questions.question: State one difference between demand and supply
questions.solution_html:
• Demand refers to the quantity of a good or service consumers are willing and able to buy, while supply
  • refers to the quantity producers are willing and able to offer for sale
  • 1 mark
  • Limited market access: Poor roads and transport isolate rural producers from markets
  • lowering income opportunities.
  • Focus on redistribution: Inspired policies like progressive taxation and social transfers to
  • reduce inequality.
  • Access to education: Improves skills and employment opportunities for marginalized groups
  • reducing income gaps.
  • Protection of land rights: Challenges displacement and exploitation caused by industrial or
  • infrastructure projects.
  • Moral judgment: Labels blame individuals instead of addressing structural causes of poverty.
  • Labour supply: Represents the number of people willing and able to work at different wage levels.
  • Minimal state intervention: The state provides welfare only when family and market systems fail.
  • Visibility and representation: Positive portrayals in media increase public awareness and
  • acceptance.
  • Inclusive climate policies: Ensure vulnerable groups (women, poor, indigenous) are
  • prioritized in adaptation plans.

questions.final_answer: prioritized in adaptation plans.

questions.question: Describe how the institutional approach addresses welfare as a normal function of society.
questions.solution_html:
• The institutional approach views welfare as a normal and integral function of society, emphasizing
  • that social services are rights of all citizens, not just charity for the poor.
  • 1 mark
  • Low investment: Inadequate electricity, water, and communication deter industries and
  • services from investing in such areas.
  • Public goods provision: Led to government investment in education, health, and sanitation to
  • improve social welfare.
  • Health and welfare services: Ensures equal access to healthcare, lowering life expectancy
  • disparities.
  • Cultural preservation: Ensures traditional practices, sacred sites, and identities are respected.
  • Policy bias: “Deserving poor” may receive aid while others are unfairly excluded.
  • Labour demand: Reflects employers’ need for workers based on productivity and business
  • conditions.
  • Conditional support: Assistance is viewed as temporary, targeting only those in dire need.
  • Challenging stereotypes: Advocacy campaigns counter myths and misconceptions about trans
  • identities.
  • Social protection schemes: Expand safety nets like insurance, cash transfers, and food aid
  • during crises.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025
questions.final_answer: during crises.

questions.question: List a factor causing racial poverty.
questions.solution_html:
• List a factor causing racial poverty.
  • Discrimination in employment and education is a major factor leading to racial poverty.
  • 1 mark
  • Restricted human capital development: Poor schools and healthcare reinforce low
  • productivity and persistent poverty.
  • 3 marks
  • Social justice principle: Influenced welfare schemes such as PDS, Mid-Day Meal, and healthcare
  • programs for equitable outcomes.
  • 3 marks
  • Gender equality initiatives: Promotes women’s empowerment and participation in economic and
  • political life.
  • Environmental conservation: Promotes sustainable resource use and opposes ecological
  • degradation.
  • Stigma and discrimination: Reinforces stereotypes and social exclusion.
  • Wage determination: The equilibrium wage is set where labour supply equals labour demand.
  • Emphasis on self-reliance: Encourages individuals to depend on work and family, not government
  • aid.
  • Policy influence: Media-driven movements push for legal protections and anti-discrimination laws.
  • Sustainable livelihood programs: Promote climate-resilient agriculture and green jobs.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025
questions.final_answer: Sustainable livelihood programs: Promote climate-resilient agriculture and green jobs.

questions.question: Describe how a developmental approach strengthens long-term welfare.
questions.solution_html:
• The developmental approach focuses on empowerment, capacity building, and economic
  • participation, which reduce dependency and strengthen long-term social welfare.
  • 1 mark

  • 5 marks

  • development planning.
  • 5 marks

  • Unemployment impact: When supply exceeds demand, unemployment rises and wages may fall.

questions.question: Identify key features of traditional economic systems.
questions.solution_html:
•  Subsistence production: Focus on meeting local and family needs rather than profit-making.
  •  Custom-based exchange: Economic roles and trade governed by traditions, norms, and bartering.
  •  Limited technological change: Slow adoption of innovation and dependence on natural resources.
  • 3 marks

questions.question: Demonstrate with examples how growth models can be critiqued
questions.solution_html:
• Demonstrate with examples how growth models can be critiqued
  • a. Neglect of inequality: Models like Rostow’s stages emphasize GDP growth but ignore social
  • disparities.
  • b. Environmental concerns: Growth-centric models overlook sustainability, as seen in
  • industrialization-driven pollution.
  • c. Cultural bias: Western models may not suit local contexts (e.g., dependency theory critique of
  • modernization).
  • d. Overreliance on markets: Neoliberal models assume trickle-down benefits that rarely reach the
  • poor.
  • e. Alternative perspectives: Human Development Index (HDI) and Sustainable Development Goals
  • (SDGs) focus on wellbeing, not just growth.
  • 5 marks
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025
questions.final_answer: Demonstrate with examples how growth models can be critiqued

questions.question: Discuss the interaction between health and economic poverty traps. Part D Essay
questions.solution_html:
• a. Poor health reduces productivity: Illness limits ability to work and earn income.
  • b. High medical costs: Out-of-pocket expenses push families deeper into poverty.
  • c. Malnutrition and low education: Weak health affects learning and long-term earning capacity.
  • d. Limited healthcare access: Rural and poor populations lack affordable medical services.
  • e. Cycle of deprivation: Poor health causes poverty, and poverty worsens health—creating a self
  • reinforcing trap.
  • 5 marks
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025
questions.final_answer: a. Poor health reduces productivity: Illness limits ability to work and earn income.
